image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Alluvial / Sankey-style flow chart** showing how total water consumption is divided into categories and subcategories.

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **flow bands** whose **width represents quantity/share**.
- Shows **hierarchical splitting** from a total into major categories, then into subcategories.
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked in the usual bar/area-chart sense; instead it uses **branching flows**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Total water consumed (“1.9 trillion gallons of water”) | Quantitative | Overall total indicated by title text; implied by full combined flow area |
| Major water-use category (Livestock, Other crops, Everything else) | Categorical/nominal | Separate flow branches/segments; text labels |
| Subcategory within major category (Cotton, Wheat, Corn grain, Barley, Other crops, Thermoelectric power, Commercial and industrial, Residential) | Categorical/nominal | Nested flow branches; text labels |
| Share of total water use (percent values such as 56%, 24%, 21%, 12%, 7%, etc.) | Quantitative | Flow width/area; percentage labels |
| Water volume in gallons (e.g., 1,064 billion gallons; 448 billion gallons; 387 billion gallons) | Quantitative | Text labels for major categories |
| Hierarchical relationship / grouping (subcategory belonging to a major category) | Ordinal/structural grouping | Branching/nesting of flows from parent category |

comments.raw_comment:
The graph shows what the 1.9 trillion gallons of water from the Colorado River consumed by humans every year is used for. A solid majority of it goes into the process of raising livestock, and another smaller, yet still substantial, slice goes into other forms of agriculture. Very little of the water goes directly towards humans.
I wonder why anyone hasn't made a way to reduce the amount of water that livestock takes up. It's very plain to see that animals require a lot of money to be raised into a viable resource. They need water for the animals to drink and to use for raising their feed. 
This is important to me, as a decline in the Colorado River means a lack of water that fuels many people's livelihoods, as well as the market. This could result in many people having to move and and ending up losing jobs. It would also result in a decrease in the availability of some livestock products and food staples.
TITLE: WESTERN STATES SIZZLING

comments.raw_comment:
This graph uses a visual depiction of a blue "river" splitting into various "tributaries" to represent the amount of actual water from the Colorado river that is consumed for each labeled purpose. The width of each "tributary" is proportional to the volume of water used for that purpose.

We wonder why there is a narrow strip that splits off of the livestock branch, appearing as if it would merge with the "other crops" branch, but later rejoins the livestock branch. Although it might simply be a visual artifact, we nevertheless noticed that the livestock and other crops branches are conceptually linked in several ways. For example, much of the water associated with raising livestock comes from irrigation of feed crops: we wonder whether this component was included in the livestock section or the "other crops" section, as corn is widely used for both human and livestock consumption. Corn is particularly relevant to my community, as it is one of the principal crops grown in Champaign County (along with soybeans).

"A Tribute to the Tributaries of Water Consumption"

comments.raw_comment: In this graph, the consumption of water from the Colorado River is examined. This graph illustrates what percentage of the total 1.9 trillion gallons of water being used is allotted to which industries. The Colorado River is a huge source of water for people, crops, animals, and power for the entire Western portion of America. In recent years, the rivers' flow has decreased. As seen in this graph, the river's water is used for varying reasons that support life. It is relied upon by millions of people to sustain their food, power, clothes, drinking water, and more. Interestingly, most of the water ends up being used by livestock, an interesting fact I thought was unexpected. I think the most important part of this graph is how it outlines that this river is vitally important to countless aspects of life. If problems persist and this river is no longer available for use, it could be detrimental to life in the West. I think this graph could be called "Say Thank You to The Colorado River."

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the majority of water, 1,064 billion gallons, is consumed by livestock. I also notice that the least amount of water, 387 billion gallons, is consumed by commerical and industrial use, residential use, and thermoelectric power. It makes sense that the majority of water is consumed by livestock, as access to water is necessary for them to survive and produce money. Water is central to the existence of both livestock and crops, which is why they consume the greatest amount of water out of the three categories presented. I wonder however why it does not specify what livestock consumes a given percentage of the water, as it does for the other two categories. I wonder if increases in global warming will cause many of these categories to not have enough water to survive. This relates to my community as the supply of water we have contributes directly to the amount of crops, livestock, and clothing that are produced, basic things that are in our every day lives.  
Gallons Galore

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I noticed that out of the 1.9 trillion gallons of water that are consumed from the Colorado river, livestock takes up the majority of water usage (56%). It seems that the agricultural industry takes up most of the water supply, as the second highest usage is for other crops (24%)

What do you wonder?

I wonder if there is a greater way to lessen the use of water in the agricultural industry, apart from what everyday people can do to limit water usage and cut down on livestock consumption. It is also possible that global warming has further contributed to the shrinkage.

How does this relate to you and your community?

Water is a finite resource, and those communities that rely on the Colorado river are not the only ones experiencing the impact of depleting water supplies. As mentioned previously, water conservation methods and veganism are both verifiable methods to reduce water consumption. 

"Where's my water? No longer a game"

comments.raw_comment:
This graph demonstrates where the 1.9 trillion gallons of water per year taken from the Colorado River are distributed. It shows that 56% goes to livestock, 24% goes to other crops (cotton, wheat, corn, grain, barley, etc.), and 21%  goes to everything else (residential, commercial industrial, and thermoelectric power).  The Colorado River is shrinking rapidly. If it dries out, it would cause a catastrophe in the West. By analyzing this graph, we can see how to reduce our use of the water from the Colorado River.  The caption says that the Colorado River provides water for over 40 million people. I wonder in which category this statistic is factored into the graph. I assume that this would be included in either commercial or residential use. These two categories take up a tiny percentage of the Colorado River water each year. While we can attempt to reduce our daily intake of water, the larger consumers of water must be addressed first. Reducing our water use on animals and plants will make a bigger difference. I notice that over half of the water is devoted to livestock. We need to find ways to make this water use more sustainable. We could install more desalinization plants in the US to try and compensate for the lack of fresh water we have left. This could help reduce the use of water for livestock and crops as they could live off of desalinated freshwater. The shrinking rates of fresh water will become an increasingly prominent problem.
“Colorado River to Colorado Creek”

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts how water is allocated for different purposes. The vast majority of water is sent to residences. The other largest purpose is cotton. This shows how water is an important part of the Earth's infrastructure and product creation. Plants need water to grow, but the majority of water is being put into buildings and clothing rather than crops. This information could help in taking pollution and the ecosystem's health into consideration. As water is being used to work in industry, the water is not being as heavily allocated to natural purposes. I wonder why it is so heavily used in industry and not farming. It seems counter intuitive. This is relevant to me as water pollution and industry are two big topics. As my generation comes into positions of power, we will have to modify how the world functions in order to keep it healthy. I would call this graph "How are we using our water?"

This means that the majority of the Colorado River’s resources, or approximately 1,064 billion gallons of water, are provided to farm animals in the west. Therefore, I think that livestock is a main contributor to the Colorado River shrinking due to an excessive expenditure of water. With this, I wonder if the fact that there is a rising demand for food in the United States leads to an increase in livestock in the West, thus resulting in the necessity of more resources (like water) to livestock operations. Also, I am curious about how the distribution of water from the Colorado River has changed over time, especially in terms of the climate crisis? In general, the graph relates to my community as I am an American. The shrinking supply of water in the Colorado River can result in a catastrophe in the agriculture industry and electricity in the west, impacting the lives of others in the United States. A headline that captures the graph’s main idea could be “The Colorado River Is Running Out of Water”

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support
it?

This graph shows how water in the Colorado River is distributed to different industries and purposes. I notice that the majority of water goes to livestock and crops. This makes sense because Colorado is in the midwest, near many states that have a major agricultural economy, like Nebraska and Kansas. I notice that in the "livestock" section of the chart, there is a slight, thin breakaway from the larger portion. I wonder why this is and what it represents. I also notice that the total amount of water that is taken from the river is 1.9 trillion gallons. This is a huge amount, and I wonder how this usage will affect the future of the river. I wonder if as the population, economy, and consumption grows in the America, this will became a negative effect on the river and resources will deplete. This especially relates to me and my community because the population of Earth is growing rapidly fast and it is important for us to secure our future with enough resources.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph displays the 1.9 trillion gallons of water which is the amount consumed within the Colorado River basin in a typical year. That's a lot of water! There are 3 categories of what uses all of the water: Livestock, Other Crops, and Everything else. I notice that on the graph in the dark blue thick strip, Livestock is 56% and uses 1.064 billion gallons of water, making it the largest user/consumer of water compared to the other 2 groups shown. I also notice how in total the Other Crops is 24% and uses 448 billion gallons of water but inside out of the wheat, corn grain, barley, and other crops, cotton has the highest consumption percentage at 11%. This shows how the production of cotton requires a large amount of water. I wonder why the last category Everything else surprised me because the residential use consumption percentage was only 12% and I would expect it to be higher. I would expect it to be higher because many residential homes use a lot of water on a daily basis when using a shower, running water, or a well filtration system, etc. This relates to me and my community because I am a resident of a home and I take hot showers and I have a well system which is where my family gets its filtered water from, which I drink from every single day. This also brought to my attention the amount of water that I may use on a daily basis which makes me more aware to use less to lower my parents water bill and to save more water.

This graph shows how many gallons of water various categories consume from the Colorado River. The Colorado River, containing 1.9 trillion gallons of water, is an imperative source to fuel everyday life for millions of people. Of the annual consummtion average, 56% (1,064 bil gal) is consumed by livestock, 24% (448 bil gal) is consumed by a multitude of crops, and 21%(387 bil gal) is consumed by electricity, industrial, or residential use. In recent years, the river has dropped to one-third of its normal size. This has been linkedmto population growth and climate change. I wonder which more of an impact. Climate change is rapid and has affected ecosystems all around the world. I wonder if overconsumption linked to increasing population has hurt the Colorado River more than climate change. If the river’s flow rate proceeds to drop,will it remain a sustainable source? If not, I wonder how it will affect the surrounding communities. If it is to affect industrial companies, this could impact the American economy as a whole. In my own community, my county has two sustainable sources of water from rivers. However, we have experienced the wettest year to date but the driest October in over 100 years. This has made it difficult for farmers, who occupy most of the land, to maintain strong crops. While we have not dealt with decreasing access to river water supply, climate change’s impact on rainfall has hurt a main source of trade and income.

“As It Flows, Where Must Our Water Go?”

This relates to my community because even though I don’t live near the Colorado River, it is important to try to limit my daily water consumption as much as possible to help with problems like these. My headline for this graph would be: “With Record High Water Consumption, Will the Colorado River Remain?”

comments.raw_comment:
What I Notice:
I notice that 1.9 trillion gallons of water is consumed within the Colorado River Basin in a typical year. This information shocked me as I did not know that that much water was used from this river. I notice that livestock use most of the water (56%). Also, how cotton uses more water than wheat, corn grain, barley, and other crops.

What I Wonder:
Why does livestock consume most of the water? Why has climate change dropped the Colorado River Basin’s flow? What other uses does water provide to the world? Why does cotton use more water than wheat, corn grain, barley, and other crops? What renewable sources of energy can help protect water and supposedly replace it? How much of the water is consumed by humans? What is causing the Colorado River to dry up so quickly?

How This Relates to Me and My Community: 
This relates to me and my community because humans use a lot of water. The Colorado River “supplies drinking water to 40 million Americans in seven Western states.” This shows that this river provides people in the United States with a crucial water source. Without it, we would not be able to survive. Furthermore, in order to protect this water, we must not waste it and prevent it from becoming polluted. Water makes up 70% of the human body, which is why, without it, we would die. Also, only 1.2 percent of Earth's water can be consumed by humans which is why we must use it wisely.

1) What do you notice?
I noticed that of the 1.9 trillion gallons of water consumed in the Colorado River basin, most of it is going into livestock. 1,064 billion gallons of water go into livestock, using 56 percent of the total water used in a year. Other crops use 24 percent of the total water used in the Colorado River, using 448 billion gallons of water. Everything else like residential homes and commercial buildings uses 24 percent of the water. Cotton accounts for 11 percent of the total water used, accounting for almost half of the total percent of crop’s water use. Residential usage accounts for 12 percent of the water used, with it accounting for the most usage of water aside from crops and livestock. 

2) What do you wonder? 
I wonder why Cotton uses so much water compared to other crops. I also wonder how much water different livestock animals use. 

3) How does this relate to you and your community? 
This relates to me and my community because if the Colorado River dries up it will affect the national economy and food supply. Since it supplies a lot of water to the livestock and crop industries, it will affect the prices of meat and other produce in the United States. 

4) What’s going on in this graph? 
Billion Gallons Gone Per Year: Livestock is drinking dry the Colorado River

I wonder why livestock uses so much water (56%), when only 12% is used on humans. How is it that we are using more water on the livestock we grow than on ourselves?

This goes to show the impact that  fostering livestock has on our water systems. When a time comes where we begin to have a deficit of water, we will have to begin optimizing this water usage so that livestock does not take such a large portion, and water use decreases or even leaves more room for crops or residential areas / industrial purposes.

In New Jersey, water is usually taken from neighboring states in order to provide for us which is astounding since we have one water source providing many states. 1. I notice that the majority of water from the Colorado River that is used each year is consumed or used for livestock. I think this is very surprising, and also concerning, seeing that there are people and crops who also need the water.

2. I wonder how livestock production could better manage their water consumption in order to preserve the river's resources. The amount of water that they consume each year is staggering, and I feel that with better management they could leave more water for others.

3. This strongly relates to our community, because living in Colorado there are many debates on who gets the water from the Colorado River, and seeing this graph I can see why. There are lots of arguements about which states need to use water from the Colorado River, and how much. California wants to use the water from the river, but because of the shortages they are only able to use a little bit, causing them to have to cut back on water usage. However, is this really necessary when the main user of the water is livestock? Can we manage our resources better to prevent this so that everyone can have water?

4. It May Be Time For Meatless Monday

comments.raw_comment:
What I noticed
This graph demonstrates how the water in the Colorado River is being distributed. The main amount of water is being used for livestock and crops. Everything else like residents, commercial industrial, and thermoelectric power is only using 21%.  The residents have a total of 12% of the actual water (158.25 billion gallons). 

So What?
Because of the shrinking river, this means all the proportions are becoming less and smaller but still staying the same. An incoming problem could be the rise in the Colorado population in the past ten years might affect the water proportions with more demand for water to residents. Another problem could be the high amounts of salt inside the soil not letting the water to the crops. This will require more percentage toward crops to increase. A great solution to this is to let other parts of the country create cotton opening up 12% of the river water to other causes.

Title "Decreasing Colorado River"
